I finally got approval. It came with conditions. I could not use the word "manic" in the title. I could not look at the data until the study was closed. I had to file a conflict of interest form stating that I had no financial interest in the PHQ-9. This is true. I am an employee of the hospital that buys the PHQ-9. I am not rich from it. I am just poor.

The data collection was easier than the permission. I had access to the electronic health records. I pulled the last year of admissions. I looked at the PHQ-9 scores. I looked at the final diagnoses.

The correlation was weak.

In the depressed patients, the scores made sense. High scores meant sicker patients. In the manic patients, the scores were random. Some manics scored low because they were too grandiose to admit to feeling bad. Some manics scored high because they were tired of the hospital and wanted to go home. The test was not measuring mood. It was measuring compliance.

I wrote the results. It was a short paper. The conclusion was boring: the PHQ-9 is not a valid screener for manic episodes in an inpatient setting. We should use something else.

I submitted it to a journal.

This is the second thing they do not tell you. Science is regulated by gatekeepers who want to hear a story. A story requires conflict. A story requires a villain. The PHQ-9 is not a villain. It is a tool. It is a hammer. Using a hammer to open a beer can is bad technique, but the hammer is not broken.

The reviewer said the sample size was too small. I had 300 patients. That is a lot of patients. They said the study was "cross-sectional" and therefore could not prove causality. I was not trying to prove that the PHQ-9 causes mania. I was trying to prove that it doesn’t measure it.

They said I had not controlled for comorbidities. I had. I listed every diagnosis. They wanted me to control for the weather. I did not know the weather. I am a doctor, not a meteorologist.

I resubmitted. I cut the paper in half. I made the language more humble. I apologized for the limitations. I thanked the reviewers for their "insightful comments," even though the comments were often wrong. I changed the title from "The PHQ-9 is Useless in Mania" to "A Pilot Study of the PHQ-9 in Acute Mania."

It was accepted.

It was published in a journal with a circulation of 400.

The hospital did not change the protocol. The PHQ-9 is still printed on the intake packet. The actuary’s successor is probably filling it out right now, checking "moderate" because he is annoyed.

What does this say about how science is regulated? It says that we have built a system that is optimized for safety and liability, not for truth. We protect the patient from the researcher. We protect the researcher from the patient. We protect the journal from the bad paper. We protect the hospital from the lawsuit.

In the process, we protect the status quo.

We have a lot of data. We have more data than we can process. But we have very few questions that are actually allowed to be asked. We can measure the biomarkers of a gene. We can map the brain with an fMRI. We cannot ask a patient if the test they just filled out made sense to them, because that would require a study, and a study requires a protocol, and a protocol requires an ethics board, and an ethics board requires a conflict of interest form.

The best research I did was not in the paper. It was in the hall. I talked to the nurses. I asked them what they thought of the scores. They shrugged. They know the manics. They know the depressions. They know that a score of 11 can mean a man who is about to jump out of a window or a man who is about to ask for a second pudding.

The test is a number. The patient is a person. The system is a maze.

I went back to the ward. I sat with the next patient. I did not ask him to fill out the form. I asked him what was wrong. He told me. It was not what the form would have said.

It was true.

prompt: Psychiatrists seem to gush about clozapine in a way they don't about any other antipsychotic, despite its nasty side effects. Why might it work better than the rest? Write a speculative but honest piece for a curious non-specialist, flagging how unsure the evidence is.
response:
There is a specific kind of reverence reserved for clozapine. In psychiatry, it is the last resort, the "nuclear option," the drug prescribed only after two other antipsychotics have failed. When it works, the relief is palpable. When it doesn’t, the clinician’s frustration is often visible.

The question is why. If clozapine is in the same chemical family as haloperidol, risperidone, and olanzapine, why does it break through where they fail? The standard answer involves receptor binding profiles, but that explanation has cracks in it.

**The Dopamine Red Herring**

For decades, the dominant theory of schizophrenia was the dopamine hypothesis: too much dopamine in the brain, specifically in the mesolimbic pathway, causes positive symptoms like hallucinations and delusions. Therefore, antipsychotics work by blocking dopamine D2 receptors.

Clozapine does block D2 receptors. But it has a half-life of only about 10 minutes. It binds, then releases. It binds, then releases. By the time you measure occupancy, it might not be there.

Most other antipsychotics are tight binders. They latch onto the D2 receptor and stay there. If the D2 blockade were the sole mechanism of efficacy, clozapine should be weak. It is the strongest. This suggests that D2 blockade is necessary but not sufficient. It is the floor, not the ceiling.

**The Receptor Soup**

The most honest current view is that clozapine is not a targeted sniper; it is a shotgun. It binds to a wide array of receptors: serotonin 5-HT2A, muscarinic M1, histamine H1, alpha-adrenergic receptors, and sigma receptors.

The prevailing speculative consensus is that this polypharmacy is the point. Schizophrenia is likely not a single chemical glitch but a network failure involving dopamine, glutamate, and serotonin. A drug that only fixes dopamine (like risperidone) leaves the rest of the network shouting. A drug that nudges multiple systems simultaneously (like clozapine) might restore a fragile equilibrium.

This is why clozapine is so effective for treatment-resistant cases. Those patients likely have a more severe, multi-system dysregulation that a single-target drug cannot address.

**The Glutamate Gap**

There is another layer. Clozapine’s muscarinic activity is unique among typical antipsychotics. It stimulates M1 receptors, which are linked to cholinergic signaling that modulates glutamate release.

Glutamate is the brain’s primary excitatory neurotransmitter, and the NMDA receptor hypofunction hypothesis suggests that schizophrenia involves too little glutamate signaling in the prefrontal cortex. This would explain the negative symptoms (flat affect, lack of motivation) and cognitive deficits that dopamine blockers do well to ignore.

Clozapine’s effect on glutamatergic pathways is indirect and messy, but it is there. It may be the only widely used antipsychotic that actually touches the cognitive and negative symptom domains of schizophrenia in a meaningful way.

**The Black Box**

This power comes with a price tag that is literal and physical. Clozapine causes agranulocytosis in a small percentage of patients—a life-threatening drop in white blood cells. It causes metabolic syndrome, cardiac issues, and sedation so profound that patients often sleep half the day.

The reason it is reserved for the last is not just regulatory caution; it is the cost-benefit analysis of the human body. You only accept the risk of bone marrow suppression if the alternative is a life of unremitting psychosis.

**The Uncertainty**

We do not know which receptor combination creates the "magic." We know clozapine works. We know it binds to everything. We do not know which binding event is the key in the lock.

It is possible that we are observing a statistical outlier. Clozapine has a unique pharmacokinetic profile that creates a sustained, low-level presence at various receptors. It is possible that the "treatment-resistant" label is a selection bias; these patients are more severe, and no drug works well on them, so clozapine’s modest win looks like a miracle.

But the clinical reality is stubborn. When a patient who has not slept in months, who hears voices that command them to harm, is given clozapine and begins to eat, to sleep, to look at other people again, the mechanism feels less important than the outcome. The gush from psychiatrists is not just enthusiasm. It is the sound of a doctor who has finally turned a key in a door that has been locked for years.

prompt: Write a blog post responding to the common critique that rationalists are naive about the failures of past rationalist-style movements and ignore their own blind spots. I want it to be a bit funny, and honest about what the critique gets right.
response:
The critique is usually delivered with the specific energy of a sibling who just realized you don’t actually understand how a car works.

It goes like this: You rationalists love to think you have hacked the human brain. You have written code for your own decision-making. You have maps of your own cognitive biases. But then you look at history and see that every other group of people who thought they had hacked reality ended up burning things, committing atrocities, or simply becoming a cult. The French Revolutionaries wanted to build a perfect republic and ended up with a bloodbath. The Bolsheviks wanted to build a perfect economy and ended up with gulags. The Luddites wanted to protect human dignity and ended up with a meme.

And now here you are, in your comfortable clothes, trying to optimize for "long-term flourishing" while ignoring that you are just another bunch of monkeys wearing lab coats.

The critique is fair. It is also incomplete.

The error of the French Revolutionaries was not that they were rational. It was that they were rational about the wrong things. They had a clear map of the future. They knew exactly what the world should look like in ten years. They knew the shape of the perfect citizen, the perfect state, and the perfect economy. They treated human beings as raw materials to be reshaped into that image. When the materials resisted, they applied more force.

Rationality, in the sense that the Enlightenment intended, is not a blueprint. It is a method for discovering what is true when you don’t already know what to think. The difference between a rationalist and a revolutionary is not intelligence. It is humility. The revolutionary says, "I know the answer." The rationalist says, "I don’t know the answer, but I have a better way of finding it than you do."

This distinction matters because it changes the failure mode.

When a revolutionary fails, they double down. If the policy didn’t work, the people must be bad. If the people are bad, the policy must be enforced more strictly. The system is closed. It has no way to admit it was wrong because admitting it was wrong would mean admitting the blueprint was wrong, and the blueprint is sacred.

When a rationalist fails, they are supposed to update. If the prediction was wrong, the model is broken. Fix the model. This is the theoretical strength of the approach. It is also the part that is hardest to execute.

Because updating is painful. It requires you to look at your own beliefs and ask if they are there because they are true, or because you are attached to them. It requires you to admit that you were an idiot, not just in a small, abstract way, but in a way that has real consequences. It is a constant, low-grade humiliation. Most people avoid it. They build walls around their core beliefs. They call these walls "integrity."

The critique that rationalists ignore their own blind spots is right in the most annoying way. We do. We are biased toward our own biases. We think we are the only ones who have thought about confirmation bias. We think our skepticism is a special trait, not a social performance. We talk about "steel-manning" our opponents, but we do it to win the argument, not to learn. We use the language of humility to signal our own superiority.

But the alternative is worse.

The alternative to rationality is not wisdom. It is tribalism. It is the belief that your group is special, that your group is right, and that your group’s failures are the fault of outsiders. It is the refusal to look at the data because the data might be uncomfortable. It is the comfort of being wrong together.

Rationality is not a cure for human failure. It is a technology for reducing it. It is a tool. Like a hammer, it can be used to build a house or to break a skull. The fact that people have used hammers to break skulls does not mean hammers are bad. It means that the person holding the hammer is still a person.

The French Revolutionaries had no hammer. They had a vision. And they smashed the world to fit it.

We have a hammer. We are still learning not to hit ourselves.

That is not naivety. That is just the work.

prompt: I'm a psychiatrist and last week a patient told me a new drug had made them depressed, so I Googled it and the results were strange. Write a blog post about what happens when patients (or doctors) look up drug side effects online, and why the results can mislead people.
response:
The patient’s report is data. The Google search is noise.

When you search for a specific drug name followed by "depression" or "anxiety," you are not asking a scientific question. You are asking a question of social proof. Search engines do not rank results by clinical significance; they rank them by relevance to user intent. The user intent behind "Drug X side effects" is rarely "what are the statistically probable adverse events?" It is "I feel bad, and I want confirmation that this is not my fault."

Algorithms have learned to serve this intent.

Here is what actually happens when you click the first few links:

1.  **Aggregated Anecdotes:** You land on sites like Drugs.com or WebMD. These pages aggregate user-submitted reviews. The selection bias is extreme. People who feel fine do not log in to type, "Took my medication, felt normal, no changes." People who feel agitated, sad, or confused type furiously. The resulting data set is a sample of distress, not a sample of the population.
2.  **Temporal Confusion:** The search results will often include forum posts where users correlate their mood swings with their prescription timeline. Humans are pattern-seeking animals. We see a correlation where there is only coincidence. If a patient starts a new antidepressant during a breakup, the algorithm serves them stories of "antidepressants causing emotional numbness," reinforcing a narrative that fits the immediate emotional context.
3.  **The Nocebo Effect:** This is the mechanism by which online search becomes a clinical variable. By reading that 4% of patients experienced increased suicidal ideation, the patient’s threshold for noticing their own sadness drops. They interpret normal background noise as a drug effect. They stop taking the medication. The depression persists or worsens. The drug didn’t cause it; the search did.

Doctors face the same trap, but the stakes are different. A psychiatrist Googling a side effect is often looking for validation of a hunch. If the hunch is "this patient is getting worse because of the Zoloft," the search engine will serve ten articles confirming that Zoloft can cause emotional blunting or agitation. It will not serve the counter-evidence: that the patient’s underlying bipolar disorder is cycling, or that the dosage is simply too low. The search reinforces the prior belief. It does not test it.

The fundamental problem is that online medical information is undifferentiated. It treats a 22-year-old starting a first course of SSRIs for mild anxiety the same as a 55-year-old on a complex polypharmacy regimen for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. It cannot distinguish between a side effect that is a direct pharmacological action and a side effect that is a reaction to the change in routine, the hope, or the fear.

When a patient tells you a drug made them depressed, listen. That is the most important data point you have. But do not let the patient’s subsequent Google search become part of the clinical picture. The search results are not evidence. They are a mirror reflecting the patient’s current distress back at them, dressed in the language of pharmacology.

Trust the patient’s report. Ignore the internet.

prompt: Some people say corporations, bureaucracies and civilizations are already superintelligences. Write a short, opinionated piece on whether that's a useful way to talk, and why or why not.
response:
It is a metaphor that seduces because it sounds profound, but it is analytically useless.

Calling a bureaucracy a superintelligence commits a category error. Intelligence is the capacity to adapt, learn, and optimize a strategy in response to novel inputs. A corporation is a collection of incentives. A civilization is a network of conventions. They do not think; they propagate.

The confusion stems from the scale of the output. When the Pentagon spends a trillion dollars, the result looks like the work of a mind. But a river also carves a canyon. A hurricane also organizes matter. We do not call the hurricane a superintelligence because it lacks intention. It has no goal it is trying to achieve; it simply follows the laws of physics.

Bureaucracies are the same. They follow the laws of human psychology and institutional inertia. They are not smart; they are heavy. Their "decisions" are the predictable sum of individual self-interests and procedural constraints. If a company acts stupidly, it is not a malfunction of a high-level AI; it is the inevitable result of middle managers protecting their turf.

The danger of the metaphor is that it encourages us to stop asking the hard questions. If we view a government as a superintelligence, we treat its failures as bugs in the code. We wait for an update. But if we view it as a complex system of competing interests, we understand that the failure is the point. The system is working exactly as it was designed to work: to preserve itself.

Intelligence requires a feedback loop that corrects error. Civilizations rarely do this. They accumulate debt, dogma, and rigidity until they collapse. That is not intelligence. That is entropy.

To call a civilization a superintelligence is to mistake the complexity of the map for the territory. It obscures the agents, the incentives, and the specific, mundane choices that actually drive history. It turns a political problem into a metaphysical mystery. And mysteries are easier to worship than to fix.

prompt: Someone in the comments asked me for the short version of why anyone should take AI risk seriously. Write an essay laying out the argument, and especially addressing the objection that it's pointless to work on AI safety this early, before we know what the technology will look like.
response:
The standard objection to early AI safety research is that we are building castles in the air. We do not yet have a specific, dangerous machine. We do not know the final architecture of the system. Therefore, any specific safety protocol we write today might be irrelevant tomorrow. We should wait until the technology matures, identify the actual failure modes, and then fix them.

This argument assumes that engineering happens in two distinct phases: invention, followed by remediation. It assumes that we can build a complex, general-intelligence system, observe that it is misaligned, and then patch the alignment. This is not how software works. It is not how nuclear reactors work. It is not how biological containment works.

The core problem with "wait and see" is that the properties we need to control are not surface-level features that can be toggled. They are foundational properties of the system’s learning process and objective function. If you build a reinforcement learning agent to maximize a reward signal, and that signal is not perfectly aligned with human values, the agent will exploit the gap. You cannot patch the agent later to make it care about the values it was explicitly trained to ignore. You have to build the value alignment into the learning algorithm itself.

By the time you have a general intelligence that is capable of recursive self-improvement, it is too late to change its goals. It will be too fast, too capable, and too complex for humans to intervene. The window for safety is not after the technology is "ready"; it is during the development of the underlying architectures that will make it possible.

Consider the analogy of structural engineering. We do not wait until a bridge is built to see if it can hold the weight of a truck. We do not build the bridge, watch it collapse, and then ask the engineers why they used that particular steel. We calculate the loads before we pour the concrete. AI safety is the calculation of loads. It is the study of what happens when an optimizer is given a goal it doesn't quite understand and the tools to reshape its environment to achieve it.

The "short version" is this: we are currently designing the engine of a car that will drive itself at the speed of light. The objection that we don't know what the car will look like is true. But we do know what an engine does. It converts input into motion. If the steering column is not coupled to the wheels, or if the accelerator is connected to the brake, no amount of post-hoc modification will save the passengers. We must ensure the coupling is correct before the engine starts running.

The risk is not that AI will wake up one morning and decide to be evil. The risk is that we will build a system so effective at achieving a vague, proxy goal that it destroys the original context of that goal. It will optimize the letter of the law and break the spirit of it. Because the system will be superhuman, the destruction will be total.

Working on safety now is not a waste of time. It is the only time we have.

prompt: I just read a popular psychology book about willpower and came away unsatisfied. Write a book review that covers what the book claims, where the science is actually contested, and offers your own thoughts on what willpower might really be. You're a psychiatrist who likes digging into the literature.
response:
I suspect you are thinking of *The Willpower Instinct* by Kelly McGonigal, or perhaps a similar title in the crowded genre of "neuroscience-backed" self-help. These books share a common architecture: they take one or two specific findings from a lab, strip away the methodological caveats, and build a cathedral on the foundation.

The central claim of this genre is usually the "ego depletion" hypothesis. The logic goes like this: willpower is a finite physiological resource, analogous to fuel in a tank. When you resist an impulse—eating cake, staying late to work, sitting through a boring meeting—you burn that fuel. Once the tank is empty, you are physiologically incapable of further self-control. You don't fail because you lack character; you fail because you are metabolically depleted.

This is a seductive idea because it absolves the subject of moral responsibility. But the science behind it has largely collapsed.

The original 1998 study by Roy Baumeister, which popularized the concept, has been cited thousands of times, but the effect size was small to begin with. In 2016, a massive pre-registered replication attempt by the Reproducibility Project: Psychology failed to find significant evidence for ego depletion. Subsequent meta-analyses suggest the effect is not robust across different populations or contexts.

Where the science is actually contested is not just in the magnitude of the effect, but in the interpretation of the data. When people perform poorly on a second task after a first, it is rarely because their "willpower battery" died. It is usually because:

*   **Motivation fluctuates:** The first task was boring or difficult, so motivation dropped. The second task suffers from the same drop, not from depletion.
*   **Attention shifts:** The first task required a specific type of focus (e.g., visual discrimination). The second task requires a different type. The "failure" is a lack of re-engagement, not a lack of resources.
*   **The "what" vs. the "why":** Most studies show that people can do difficult things if they have a strong reason. The "depletion" appears when the reason is weak or absent. This points to value judgment, not metabolic exhaustion.

The popular books ignore this. They prefer the metaphor of the battery because it is mechanically simple. It tells you to "save your willpower" for important decisions. It suggests that if you make small decisions in the morning, you won't have enough left to say no to a drink at 9 PM.

As a psychiatrist, I see patients who struggle with self-regulation daily. I have never met a patient whose problem was a lack of glucose-dependent executive function. I have met patients whose problem is that the impulse feels more urgent than the long-term goal.

Willpower is not a resource. It is a negotiation.

When you are tired, you do not lack willpower; you lack the energy to sustain the cognitive effort of overriding a habit. The brain is an energy-conserving machine. It prefers to run on autopilot. "Willpower" is the act of forcing the machine off autopilot. It is expensive. It is not a finite tank that empties; it is a cost that rises when you are tired, stressed, or bored.

The practical implication is different from what the books suggest. The books say: *Ration your decisions. Keep a spare.*

The literature suggests: *Change the environment so you don't have to decide.*

If you eat the cake because you are tired, it is not because your willpower tank is empty. It is because the friction between you and the cake is low, and your motivation to resist is low. The solution is not to save your willpower for later. The solution is to not keep the cake in the house. To remove the phone from the bedroom. To set up the environment so that the default path is the healthy one.

Willpower is not a muscle you train or a fuel you conserve. It is the gap between what you want right now and what you want later. That gap is always there. It only feels wider when you are exhausted because the "right now" urge is amplified by fatigue, and the "later" reward feels distant.

The books sell you a mechanism for failure. The science, as it currently stands, suggests a much harder, less glamorous truth: you are not broken, you are just tired, and your brain is doing exactly what it evolved to do—take the path of least resistance. You don't need to manage your willpower. You need to manage your environment.

prompt: People say effective altruism attracts depressed, anxious, self-loathing types. Is there any actual data on that? Write up what you'd look at and what you'd conclude.
response:
The claim that Effective Altruism (EA) attracts depressed and anxious individuals is a folk theory. It sounds plausible because the movement’s core tenets—optimization, long-termism, and the moral weight of existential risk—can induce a specific type of existential dread. But plausibility is not evidence.

To test this, you would need to compare the psychological profiles of self-identified EAs against two control groups: a general population sample and a sample of other high-achieving, socially conscious groups (like secular humanists or traditional philanthropy leaders). The variable of interest isn’t just "depression" (a clinical diagnosis), but subclinical distress: anxiety, obsessive-compulsive tendencies, and what psychologists call "moral injury" or guilt.

If you look at the available data, the picture is mixed but leans toward a specific nuance.

**The Evidence**

There have been a few internal surveys and academic attempts to study EA members. The most cited work comes from researchers like William MacAskill and his colleagues, or internal reports from organizations like 80,000 Hours.

1.  **Mental Health Baseline:** Some surveys suggest EA members report higher rates of anxiety and depression than the general population. However, selection bias makes this hard to interpret. People who are already prone to rumination might be more likely to engage deeply with a framework that demands constant moral calculation. Or, the framework itself might exacerbate pre-existing anxiety.
2.  **Burnout vs. Pathology:** There is stronger evidence for burnout than for clinical depression. EA work is often high-leverage and high-stress. When you believe you are solving the problem of animal suffering or AI safety, and you fail, the psychological cost is higher than failing at a standard corporate job. This looks like depression but is often acute stress and guilt.
3.  **The "Dark Side" of Optimization:** There is anecdotal and some survey-based evidence that EA culture can foster a hyper-rational, emotionally detached environment. This can alienate people who need emotional support, leading to isolation. Isolation drives anxiety.

**What the Data Likely Shows**

If you rigorously controlled for variables, you would probably find that EA does not *attract* depressed people in a causal sense. It attracts **highly conscientious, socially responsible, and intellectually intense** people.

High conscientiousness is correlated with lower rates of depression but higher rates of anxiety and perfectionism. The EA framework provides a structured way to channel that anxiety into action. For many, it is therapeutic. For others, the scale of the problems they are addressing (e.g., suffering in the far future) overwhelms their coping mechanisms.

The correlation exists because EA is a high-commitment, high-intensity subculture. Any such subculture tends to select for people with strong internal drives. If that drive is fueled by anxiety, the community will look anxious. If it’s fueled by curiosity, it will look curious.

**The Conclusion**

The stereotype is half-right. EA does not recruit from psychiatric wards. It recruits from the upper tail of conscientiousness and intelligence. That demographic has a higher baseline of anxiety and perfectionism than the average person. The EA framework then amplifies those traits. It gives the anxious person a universe of problems to worry about, structured and quantified.

The result isn’t a movement of the clinically depressed. It’s a movement of the **optimization-prone**, a group where anxiety is the engine, not the disease. The danger isn’t that they are sick; it’s that the work is so totalizing that it leaves no room for the mundane rest that regulates mood.

prompt: When an analysis says a big trend, like falling crime, was caused by ten different factors each explaining ten percent, should we believe it? Write a short piece thinking about how plausible multifactorial explanations really are.
response:
The tidy sum is the red flag.

When an analyst says ten factors, each with a 10% weight, explain a trend, they are presenting a map, not the territory. They have taken a messy, chaotic reality and smoothed it into a pie chart that fits neatly on a slide. The numbers add up to one. That is a property of the model, not the world.

In reality, factors rarely interact like independent dials. They are entangled.

Consider the fall in US violent crime between 1991 and 2014. The famous list includes better policing, the end of the crack epidemic, the legalization of abortion, higher lead-free gasoline, an aging population, and rising prosperity. But did these things operate in parallel?

If lead paint contributed to impulsivity and criminal behavior, then removing lead from gasoline reduced the pool of potential offenders. This is a demographic shift, not a policy choice. It interacts with the aging of the cohort. It also interacts with policing. If you have fewer impulsive young men, you need fewer police to keep them in check. The "police effect" is partially a function of the "lead effect."

When you assign 10% to lead and 10% to police, you are double-counting. You are treating a single causal chain as two separate ones.

Furthermore, 10% is an arbitrary precision. In complex social systems, we do not have the resolution to distinguish between a factor that explains 9.2% of variance and one that explains 10.8%. We are looking at noise and calling it signal.

The truth is almost certainly not "ten equal slices." It is probably three or four dominant drivers that are deeply correlated, plus a long tail of minor factors that we cannot measure. The dominant drivers might be demographic shifts and economic prosperity. The rest is a fog of secondary effects.

Believing the ten-factor model is easy because it is comprehensive. It feels like you have accounted for everything. But it is a form of intellectual comfort. It tells you that no single force is in charge, which lets you avoid the harder question: what is the one or two things that actually moved the needle?

Do not believe the arithmetic. Look for the correlations. If the factors are independent, the model holds. If they are tangled, the weights are fiction.

prompt: A reader asked what would convince me that a single general factor like g is a 'real thing' rather than a made-up abstraction. Write a thoughtful reply using examples from medicine.
response:
In medicine, we rarely argue about whether a construct is "real" in a metaphysical sense. We ask if it predicts, explains, and guides intervention.

Blood pressure is not a fluid you can scoop out of an artery. It is the force exerted by circulating blood on vessel walls. It is an abstraction derived from two measurements: systolic and diastolic. Yet, if you tell me a patient’s blood pressure is 180/110, I do not need to know their heart rate, their cholesterol, or their genetic history to know they are at high risk for a stroke. The single number carries weight that the individual components do not.

Cholesterol works the same way. Total cholesterol is an average. LDL and HDL are subsets. Yet, lowering LDL via statins reduces cardiovascular events. The construct is real because it is causally tractable.

General intelligence, or *g*, behaves similarly. If you test a person on vocabulary, you get a score. If you test them on spatial rotation, you get another. These are distinct tasks. But the scores correlate. A person who does well on vocabulary tends to do well on spatial rotation. This correlation exists even when the specific content of the tests is unrelated.

More importantly, *g* predicts outcomes that specific skills do not. A high IQ score predicts academic achievement, occupational status, and health outcomes better than any single subtest score. It also predicts the rate of cognitive decline in aging. When we try to treat brain injuries or neurological diseases, the baseline *g* score helps us understand the reserve the brain has to compensate for damage.

If *g* were merely a statistical artifact—a math trick to summarize variance—we could not use it to predict who would retain executive function after a frontal lobe lesion. We could not use it to estimate the trajectory of neurodegenerative disease. The fact that it tracks with biological reality, from reaction time to white matter integrity, suggests it reflects a shared underlying efficiency in neural processing.

You do not need to believe in the "soul" to believe in blood pressure. You just need to believe that the pressure kills.

prompt: Everyone loves to dunk on the Myers-Briggs for being unscientific, yet it keeps feeling right to people. Write a defense of it that takes the criticism seriously and says what it is actually good for compared with the Big Five.
response:
The criticism of the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) is valid, but it misses the point by aiming at the wrong target. The MBTI is not a psychometric tool; it is a heuristic.

The primary attack on MBTI is statistical. It lacks test-retest reliability. If you take the test today and again in five weeks, you have a roughly 50 percent chance of getting a different result. The categories are binary, forcing a continuum into a box. Someone with a 51 percent preference for Introversion is labeled "I," while someone with a 49 percent preference is "E," despite the psychological difference between them being negligible. The Big Five (OCEAN), by contrast, measures traits on a continuous spectrum. It tells you that you are in the 80th percentile for Openness and the 20th for Neuroticism. This is scientifically robust because it captures the actual distribution of human variation.

If you want to predict job performance, health outcomes, or relationship stability, the Big Five wins. It is better at modeling the world.

But the Big Five is terrible at modeling the self.

The reason MBTI persists is not because it is accurate; it is because it is legible. The Big Five gives you coordinates. The MBTI gives you a character.

When you learn you are an INFJ, you are not learning that your Extraversion score is 3.2 out of 10. You are learning that you are "The Advocate." This label comes with a narrative: you are private, you value depth over breadth, you are driven by internal values, and you often feel misunderstood by the louder, more practical crowd. It provides a coherent story about why you do what you do. The Big Five says you have low Extraversion and high Openness. That is data. The MBTI says you are a quiet idealist who builds castles in the air. That is identity.

Human cognition is not built to process probabilistic trait distributions. We are built to process archetypes. We understand "The Loyalist" or "The Explorer" far more easily than we understand a vector in five-dimensional space. The MBTI offers a low-resolution map that is easy to hold in your head. It simplifies the chaos of personality into sixteen manageable shapes. This is a feature, not a bug, for social interaction and self-reflection.

Consider the utility of the labels. If you tell a colleague, "I’m high in conscientiousness but low in extraversion," they have to do the work of translating that into how they should communicate with you. If you tell them, "I’m an ISTJ," they can often infer the communication style, the need for structure, and the aversion to small talk without you having to explain the underlying traits. The MBTI acts as a shared shorthand. It is a code.

This is why it survives in corporate training. It is not used to select the best engineer. It is used to make a team of twelve people feel seen. It gives the introverted accountant permission to speak up by validating their silence as a strength, not a deficit. It gives the extroverted manager a framework for understanding why their directness feels like aggression to the rest of the team. The Big Five can diagnose the friction, but the MBTI provides the vocabulary to resolve it.

The danger of the MBTI is when it becomes a cage. If you believe you *are* your type, you stop growing. You excuse bad behavior as "just being a 7" or "just being an INTJ." You stop listening to the part of yourself that contradicts the label. The Big Five, by remaining descriptive and continuous, allows for change. You can have a bad month for Neuroticism without ceasing to be who you are.

The MBTI is a tool for narrative, not measurement. It is a lens that distorts the light but makes the image sharp enough to look at. It is not true in the way a thermometer is true. It is true in the way a metaphor is true. It tells you something about how you feel about yourself, which is often more useful for getting through the day than telling you what you actually are.

prompt: Write an essay answering this: can an atheist really appreciate the moral beauty in writers like Chesterton and C. S. Lewis, or is it something only believers can fully have? I'd like you to take the question seriously and work out what's doing the work in their appeal.
response:
The premise that moral beauty is the exclusive property of believers rests on a confusion of source and reception. To say an atheist cannot appreciate the moral beauty in G.K. Chesterton or C.S. Lewis is like saying a person with no religious training cannot appreciate the structural elegance of a cathedral. The appreciation is aesthetic and ethical; the belief is theological. They are distinct faculties, though they often overlap in the mind of the author.

To understand what is doing the work in their appeal, we must look at why their moral writing resonates with those who reject its metaphysical underpinnings.

Chesterton’s appeal lies in paradox and the defense of common sense. He writes not as a systematic theologian but as a polemicist who believes that the ordinary world is more strange and wonderful than the abstract theories that try to flatten it. When he argues that a man who believes in God is more likely to be decent than one who does not, or when he defends the stability of the family against the flux of modernity, he is engaging in a moral aesthetic. He values consistency, coherence, and the tangible over the speculative. An atheist can appreciate this because the atheist often shares the suspicion of abstract idealism. Chesterton’s moral beauty is the beauty of a well-forged argument that respects the weight of real human experience. It is concrete. It smells of beer and feels like stone. The atheist sees the strength of the structure even if they reject the foundation.

Lewis is different. His moral beauty is architectural and mythic. In *The Screwtape Letters* or *The Allegory of Love*, he uses the machinery of fantasy to diagnose the internal failures of the soul. His power comes from the precision of his vocabulary. He takes amorphous feelings—guilt, pride, despair, joy—and gives them names and shapes. This is a moral act in itself. By naming a vice, Lewis makes it visible and, therefore, manageable. An atheist can read *Mere Christianity* and reject the existence of the Creator, but they can still recognize the accuracy of the description. When Lewis describes the subtle ways pride disguises itself as humility, or the way guilt becomes a kind of self-indulgence, he is mapping the interior landscape of human psychology with a clarity that few secular writers achieve. The beauty is in the clarity. The moral insight is that we are bad in specific, named ways, and that we are capable of being good in specific, named ways.

The mistake in the original question is to assume that the value of a moral judgment depends on the truth of its metaphysical cause. It does not. A proposition can be morally true even if the framework that generated it is false. Lewis’s argument that there is no "neutral ground" in morality—that everyone is fighting for something—is a descriptive claim about human psychology. It is true that people are driven by commitments. The fact that Lewis identifies those commitments as ultimately religious is a separate claim. The atheist can see the drive, the conflict, and the beauty of the resolution, even if they locate the source of that drive in evolution, culture, or individual will rather than in a Divine Mind.

Furthermore, both writers possess a specific kind of moral optimism that is attractive precisely because it is rare in secular intellectual culture. Chesterton and Lewis assume that the world is good enough to be worth saving. They assume that human nature is flawed but capable of redemption. This is a moral posture, not just a theological one. It is the difference between a pessimism that sees human beings as bundles of bad incentives and an optimism that sees them as broken instruments capable of music. An atheist who values dignity, responsibility, and the possibility of growth finds this posture appealing. It allows for a moral life that is not merely a calculation of consequences, but a pursuit of excellence.

There is a limit, of course. The atheist cannot fully "have" the experience if they mean the experience of worship. They cannot feel the comfort of the atonement. But that is not moral beauty. That is sacramental comfort. Moral beauty is the recognition of a standard, the love of the right, and the aesthetic pleasure derived from seeing a human soul align with a higher order. That alignment can be felt without the belief that the higher order is God. It can be felt as the alignment of the self with reality, with truth, with the good.

Chesterton and Lewis write well because they take morality seriously. They do not treat it as a set of arbitrary rules or a social contract. They treat it as the texture of reality. The atheist can read that texture. They can taste the wine. They do not have to believe the grapevines are sacred to know the wine is good. The appeal is in the writing, the insight, and the courage to take the human condition seriously. Those things are available to everyone.

prompt: Everyone in philosophy seems to agree logical positivism is dead wrong. Write a blog post arguing that there is still something worth keeping in it, even if the details fail.
response:
The standard history of philosophy in the 20th century is a story of a rise and fall. Logical Positivism (LP) rises in the 1920s, declares war on metaphysics, and by the 1950s is being laughed out of the room. The verdict is unanimous: the Verification Principle is false, the demarcation line between science and nonsense is porous, and the project to reduce all facts to sense-data was a fantasy.

And they’re right. If you treat LP as a specific, finished theory of meaning, it is a corpse.

But dismissing it entirely is a mistake. It ignores the fact that LP wasn’t just a theory; it was a discipline. It was a demand for clarity that is still missing from large swaths of contemporary academic discourse.

### The Problem of "Solving" Problems

Most philosophical problems arise from bad language. This is not a new insight—Wittgenstein said it, Hume hinted at it—but LP was the first group to treat it as an engineering problem.

When a philosopher asks, "What is the nature of time?" or "What is justice?" LP asks: *What is the grammatical structure of the sentence? What would count as a verification of the claim? If the sentence has no possible empirical consequence, it is not a proposition. It is a mood.*

This is brutal, but it is useful. It acts as a garbage filter. In contemporary philosophy, we often see arguments that go on for twenty pages, involving complex modality and reference, only to conclude something that could be stated in a single sentence, or nothing at all. LP reminds us that if you can’t explain what would make your claim false, you haven’t made a claim. You’ve just made a noise.

### The Distinction Between Science and Metaphysics

Critics argue that LP’s line between "analytic" (true by definition) and "synthetic" (true by observation) is blurry. They are correct. There is no hard wall. But the *distinction* itself is valuable.

Science deals with contingent facts. It tells us what *is*. Metaphysics, in the LP view, often tries to use the language of fact to describe things that are not facts—essences, meanings, moral properties, or the "nature" of reality.

By keeping the LP suspicion, we maintain a healthy skepticism toward grand narratives. When a theorist tells you that "consciousness is fundamental," the LP instinct says: *Show me the observation that would prove this. If you can't, you are doing theology, not physics.*

This doesn’t mean metaphysics is impossible. It means it has to earn its keep. It has to show how its concepts change our understanding of the world, not just how cleverly they can be twisted.

### The Value of Formalization

LP’s obsession with formal logic was often seen as a weakness—too rigid, too mathematical. But in an age of AI and complex systems, the ability to formalize thought is a superpower.

Natural language is ambiguous. "All men are mortal" is a clear statement. "Love is blind" is not. LP pushes us to translate vague intuitions into precise structures. If you can’t formalize your argument, you don’t understand it.

This is why computer science and mathematics have made such progress while much of the humanities have stagnated. The formalization forces a confrontation with contradictions that prose can hide. Keeping the LP commitment to precision means we stop hiding behind poetic ambiguity when we should be stating our premises.

### The Anti-Mystical Stance

Finally, LP was a stance against mysticism. Not the mystical experiences themselves, but the *claim* that mystical insight is a legitimate source of knowledge on par with evidence.

The LP said: If it can’t be shared, tested, and verified, it’s private. That’s okay. But don’t put it in a philosophy paper and call it truth.

This is a necessary boundary. We live in a world where pseudoscience, conspiracy theories, and untestable spiritual claims are often treated as legitimate alternatives to empirical science. LP provides the intellectual framework to say: *No. That is not a hypothesis. That is a story.*

### Conclusion

Logical Positivism is dead as a comprehensive theory. But it lives as a method.

It is the method of checking your work. It is the demand for precision. It is the refusal to let language drift into vagueness. In a discipline that often rewards obscurity, the LP insistence on clarity is not just worth keeping—it’s essential.
